items.passage: Earth maintained liquid water 2.7 billion years ago even though the Sun’s output was then roughly 20 percent weaker than it is today. One proposed resolution of this paradox holds that a considerably denser atmosphere retained enough heat to compensate. To evaluate that possibility, Sanjoy Som and colleagues compared fossilized raindrop imprints preserved in South African volcanic deposits of that age with impressions they made by dropping droplets of known size onto fresh ash. Because a falling drop’s terminal velocity depends on atmospheric density, the fossils indicated that the ancient air was probably only marginally denser than today’s.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It describes how researchers used traces of ancient rainfall to measure how much more faintly the Sun shone 2.7 billion years ago than it does today.
It summarizes research that used traces of ancient rainfall to show how early Earth retained enough heat to keep liquid water even though the Sun then gave off less energy than it does today.
It summarizes research that used traces of ancient rainfall to test one explanation for early Earth’s warmth and obtained a result that makes that explanation seem unlikely.
It summarizes research that used traces of ancient rainfall to compare two explanations for early Earth’s warmth and identifies which of them is better supported.
items.explanation: The text names a puzzle (liquid water when the Sun’s output was “roughly 20 percent weaker”) and one “proposed resolution”: “a considerably denser atmosphere retained enough heat to compensate.” It then describes how Som and colleagues used “fossilized raindrop imprints” to test that possibility and reports that “the ancient air was probably only marginally denser than today’s.” If the air was not much denser, the proposed explanation looks unlikely, so the text summarizes research that evaluated an explanation and produced a result that casts doubt on it, as choice C says.

A.recipe: first clause true, later clause swaps background for finding (INV)
A.why_wrong: The researchers did use traces of ancient rainfall, but what they estimated was the density of the air. The Sun’s weaker output (“roughly 20 percent”) is background the text states at the start, not something the study measured.

B.recipe: first clause true, outcome overstated (INV)
B.why_wrong: The study did use raindrop imprints, but it did not show how early Earth stayed warm. It tested one proposed resolution, “a considerably denser atmosphere,” and found the air “probably only marginally denser than today’s,” a result that weakens that explanation rather than resolving the puzzle.

D.recipe: first clause true, invented comparison (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text describes only “one proposed resolution of this paradox,” and the researchers set out “to evaluate that possibility.” No second explanation is compared, and none is identified as better supported.

sources.what: Som, Catling, Harnmeijer, Polivka, Buick 2012, Nature: raindrop imprints in 2.7-billion-year-old Ventersdorp tuffs, South Africa, compared with experimental drops into fresh and weathered ash, limit air density to less than twice modern and more probably below 1.3 kg/m3 (today 1.2), making the dense-atmosphere (pressure broadening) explanation of the faint young Sun paradox improbable

items.notes: Area: natural science (geology, early atmosphere). Key C. Key parts: 2 (research that used ancient rainfall to evaluate an explanation; result that makes it seem unlikely), the second needing an inference the passage leaves unstated. Section 6 checks: key 27 words; options 27 to 31 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: A, B and D (3 of 3). Passage softens the source (air “probably only marginally denser”), as the paper does (upper bound possible, lower estimates likely).
band7_moves: dual, hedged purpose: the key joins what the study did with what its result implies for the proposed explanation, which the passage never states outright
abstract key: “traces of ancient rainfall” and “one explanation for early Earth’s warmth” replace the passage’s nouns (imprints, ash, atmosphere)

all three distractors open with a true account of the study and fail later: A turns background (the Sun’s faintness) into the measured quantity, B invents a temperature conclusion, D reverses the result’s stance

fixes: B (invented temperature conclusion) replaced by a puzzle-solved option and D (stance-flipped twin of the key) by a two-explanations comparison, both true in their first clause
key verb “evaluate” (passage wording) changed to “test”

band7.why: P_study on 82cb7dda: two-part hedged key (tests one explanation; result makes it unlikely) needs the step from “considerably denser” to “only marginally denser”; all three distractors open true (traces of ancient rainfall) and fail later (Sun measured, puzzle solved, two explanations compared).

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Harriet Beecher Stowe’s 1862 novel The Pearl of Orr’s Island. Captain Kittridge, a former sailor who now builds boats, lives in a village on the coast of Maine.

It was said, whether slanderously or not, that the Captain’s yarns were spun to order; and as, when pressed to relate his foreign adventures, he always responded with, “What would you like to hear?” it was thought that he fabricated his article to suit his market.

But works of fiction, as we all know, if only well gotten up, have always their advantages in the hearts of listeners over plain, homely truth; and so Captain Kittridge’s yarns were marketable fireside commodities still, despite the skepticisms which attended them.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It explains the continued appeal of a character’s stories, which many suspect are invented, by suggesting that listeners prefer an entertaining tale to an accurate one.
It suggests that a character shapes his stories to please his listeners and that, once they realize this, they stop seeking his company.
It describes the doubts that a character’s stories have raised and indicates that the narrator considers those doubts unjust.
It explains the continued appeal of a character’s stories by suggesting that his listeners have no way to check his accounts of the distant places and strange events he describes.
items.explanation: The first paragraph reports the suspicion that the Captain’s “yarns were spun to order” and that “he fabricated his article to suit his market.” The second gives the reason his stories still please: “works of fiction, as we all know, if only well gotten up, have always their advantages in the hearts of listeners over plain, homely truth,” and so his yarns “were marketable fireside commodities still, despite the skepticisms which attended them.” The text therefore explains why the stories keep their appeal although listeners suspect they are invented: listeners prefer a good story to an accurate one, as choice A says.

B.recipe: first clause true, later clause reverses the outcome (REV)
B.why_wrong: It is thought that the Captain “fabricated his article to suit his market,” but listeners do not stop seeking him out: his yarns “were marketable fireside commodities still.”

C.recipe: first clause true, wrong stance given to the narrator (STANCE)
C.why_wrong: The text does describe “the skepticisms” the stories raise, but the narrator never calls them unjust. “Whether slanderously or not” leaves the question open, and the narrator goes on to call the yarns “works of fiction.”

D.recipe: key frame kept, wrong reason (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text does explain why the yarns stay popular, but the reason it gives is that “works of fiction ... have always their advantages in the hearts of listeners over plain, homely truth.” It never says listeners cannot check his accounts; it says they doubt them (“the skepticisms which attended them”).

sources.what: Stowe, The Pearl of Orr’s Island (1862), chapter V, checked against Gutenberg 31522: opening “In fact,” dropped; the next paragraph (“In short, there was no species of experience ...”) and the wife’s paragraph omitted before “But works of fiction”

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1862). Key A. Key parts: 2 (the stories stay popular despite doubt; why: fiction pleases more than plain truth). Section 6 checks: key 19 words; options 19 to 24 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: B, C and D (3 of 3). Short abstract key in the manner of b0f7541b. Adapted: “In fact,” dropped at the start; two intervening paragraphs omitted; dialect apostrophes none in the excerpt.
band7_moves: archaic, periodic prose (1862) whose point is carried by an aside (“whether slanderously or not”) and a generalization (“as we all know”) that the key must fold together
short abstract key (“a character’s stories”, “makes them up”) with no passage nouns, as in b0f7541b
B, C and D each keep a true first half (tailoring stories; the doubts; adapting to the audience) and fail later (listeners leave; narrator calls the doubts unjust; he believes them himself)

fixes: key rewritten to name the reason the text gives (listeners prefer an entertaining tale to an accurate one), away from the passage’s “still, despite” wording
D (wholly invented belief, which the cut paragraph actually voices through his wife) replaced by the key’s frame with a reason the text does not give (listeners cannot check his accounts)
explanation and why_wrong rewritten

band7.why: P_lit on b0f7541b: 1862 periodic prose; abstract key carries the suspicion and the reason; D keeps the key’s frame with a reason the text does not give, B and C open true and fail on the outcome and on the narrator’s stance.

items.passage: The survival of an immense seed collection in Leningrad (now Saint Petersburg) during World War II is frequently cited as an extraordinary demonstration of scientific devotion. Assembled largely through botanist Nikolai Vavilov’s expeditions in search of crop varieties, the collection was housed at the research institute that now bears his name. Throughout the city’s nearly 900-day siege, the institute’s staff safeguarded approximately 120 tonnes of seeds, nuts, and roots against incendiary bombs, freezing temperatures, and rodents, as well as against their own hunger; <u>at least 19 of them died, mostly from starvation</u>.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It indicates a human cost of the siege in order to explain why the collection’s survival is frequently cited as a symbol of the endurance shown by the city’s residents.
It conveys how severe conditions were in the besieged city, supporting the claim that hunger did more harm to the collection than bombing did.
It specifies a cost of protecting the collection, suggesting that the effort to save it was less successful than it is frequently said to have been.
It reinforces the text’s opening characterization of the collection’s survival by indicating the price that some of the staff paid for guarding the seeds.
items.explanation: The first sentence says the collection’s survival “is frequently cited as an extraordinary demonstration of scientific devotion.” The last sentence says the staff safeguarded the seeds “as well as against their own hunger,” and the underlined portion adds that “at least 19 of them died, mostly from starvation.” Those deaths show how much the staff gave up rather than eat the collection, so the portion reinforces the opening characterization of the collection’s survival, as choice D says.

A.recipe: first clause true, characterization swapped (SWAP)
A.why_wrong: The deaths are a human cost of the siege, but the text does not present the collection’s survival as a symbol of the residents’ endurance; it says the survival is cited as “an extraordinary demonstration of scientific devotion.”

B.recipe: first clause true, invented comparison (INV)
B.why_wrong: The portion does reflect harsh conditions, but the text never compares the harm done by hunger with the harm done by bombs; it lists “incendiary bombs, freezing temperatures, and rodents” and hunger as threats the staff guarded against.

C.recipe: first clause true, cost read as failure (REV)
C.why_wrong: The portion does specify a cost, but the text never suggests the effort fell short: the staff “safeguarded approximately 120 tonnes” of material through the siege, and the deaths support, rather than question, the description of the effort as “an extraordinary demonstration of scientific devotion.”

sources.what: Vavilov Institute of Plant Industry: during the Siege of Leningrad staff protected the seeds from fire bombs, cold, rodents and their own hunger; at least 19 died, mostly from starvation; the collection of some 120 tonnes of seeds, nuts and roots survived

items.notes: Area: history (history of science, World War II). Key D. Key parts: 2 (underscores the devotion named in sentence 1; by showing the cost to the staff). Span role: a means (a figure of extent), not the claim. Section 6 checks: key 21 words; options 21 to 25 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: A, B and C (3 of 3). Siege length rounded (872 days as nearly 900).
band7_moves: underlined figure whose job is extent, tied to the evaluative claim two sentences earlier (“an extraordinary demonstration of scientific devotion”), as in 2e744883
every distractor opens with a true description of the figure (a cost, severe conditions, the number who died) and invents what the text does with it
key paraphrases the span (“what guarding the collection cost”) instead of restating the deaths

fixes: key no longer repeats “devotion” from sentence 1 (now “reinforces the text’s opening characterization”)
A (invented abandonment) replaced by a swapped characterization (symbol of the residents’ endurance), C (crude reversal) by cost read as failure
explanation and why_wrong rewritten

band7.why: F_example on 2e744883 and 9b01bcf4: the span is a means (a figure of cost) whose job depends on the first sentence’s characterization, which the key names without repeating; all three distractors open true and fail on the later clause (residents’ endurance, hunger against bombs, failure).

items.passage: Composed anonymously in Fatimid Egypt between roughly 1020 and 1050 CE, the Book of Curiosities of the Sciences and Marvels for the Eyes is a cosmography, an illustrated treatise describing both the heavens and the terrestrial world. A copy produced in the early thirteenth century, acquired by Oxford’s Bodleian Library in 2002, contains seventeen maps, most of them extremely rare, including the earliest recorded map of Sicily and a rectangular world map that is the earliest surviving map to incorporate a graphic scale. Such diagrams document how geographic knowledge was transmitted from Greek and Syriac traditions into early Islamic scholarship.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe a medieval work and explain how its world map changed the way European mapmakers represented distance
To describe a medieval work and explain what its maps reveal about the history of geographic knowledge
To explain why a medieval manuscript was copied in the thirteenth century and later acquired by a library in England
To argue that the maps in a medieval manuscript relied on Greek and Syriac sources rather than on direct observation
items.explanation: The text first describes the Book of Curiosities: when and where it was composed, what kind of work it is, and the surviving copy with its “seventeen maps.” It then points to two notable maps and ends by saying that “such diagrams document how geographic knowledge was transmitted from Greek and Syriac traditions into early Islamic scholarship.” Choice B covers both the description of the work and what its maps reveal.

A.recipe: first half true, overreach in the second (BROAD)
A.why_wrong: The text does describe the work, and it says the world map is the earliest surviving map “to incorporate a graphic scale,” but it never says the map changed how European mapmakers showed distance.

C.recipe: partial and invented cause (PART)
C.why_wrong: The text mentions that the copy was made in the thirteenth century and acquired in 2002, but it does not explain why either happened, and these details are only part of its description of the work.

D.recipe: stance and overreach from the last sentence (STANCE)
D.why_wrong: The text says the maps show how knowledge “was transmitted from Greek and Syriac traditions,” but it does not argue a point, and it never contrasts those sources with direct observation.

sources.what: Book of Curiosities: anonymous Fatimid Egyptian cosmography composed 1020 to 1050, copy of the early 13th century acquired by the Bodleian Library in 2002; 17 maps, 14 extremely rare, including the earliest recorded map of Sicily and a rectangular world map that is the earliest surviving map with a graphic scale; shows transmission of geographical knowledge from Greek and Syriac traditions into early Islamic scholarship

items.notes: Area: history (history of cartography). Key B. Planned band_target 7, written as band 6: P_profile has no band-7 official item (spec/rw/band7/text_structure_and_purpose.md; 3.13 and 3.18 are band 6), per WAVE.md. Band-6 moves: dense content and near misses in scope (A overreaches the graphic-scale detail into an influence on Europe; C takes two details for the purpose; D turns the last sentence into an argument). “14 of 17 extremely rare” given as “most of them”.

band7.why: P_profile has no band-7 official item (3.13 and 3.18 are band 6), so it cannot be band 7; dense content and scope near misses make it a strong band 6.

items.passage: When Darwinius masillae, a strikingly complete 47-million-year-old primate skeleton from Germany, was unveiled in 2009, it was widely publicized as a key link in the evolution of monkeys, apes, and humans. Within months, however, Erik Seiffert and colleagues compared 360 anatomical features across 117 living and extinct primates and placed Darwinius among an extinct group whose closest living relatives are lemurs and lorises, attributing the traits it shares with monkeys to convergent evolution. A nearly intact skeleton, the case suggests, does not by itself settle where a species belongs in evolutionary history.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It presents the reassessment of a celebrated fossil to argue that the early publicity it received led researchers to overlook the specimen’s most important features.
It describes how a celebrated fossil was reclassified to show that monkeys and apes are more closely related to lemurs than researchers once believed.
It describes how a celebrated fossil was reclassified to show that traits shared by distantly related primates usually result from convergent evolution.
It discusses a celebrated fossil’s reclassification to illustrate that even an exceptionally preserved specimen may not reveal how a species is related to others.
items.explanation: The text reports that Darwinius, “a strikingly complete” skeleton, was publicized “as a key link in the evolution of monkeys, apes, and humans,” and that Seiffert and colleagues then placed it with relatives of “lemurs and lorises.” The last sentence draws the lesson: “A nearly intact skeleton, the case suggests, does not by itself settle where a species belongs in evolutionary history.” The text thus discusses the reclassification to illustrate that even an exceptionally preserved specimen may not reveal how a species is related to others, as choice D says.

A.recipe: right case, invented purpose (INV)
A.why_wrong: The text does present the reassessment of a celebrated fossil, but it never says the publicity caused researchers to overlook any features; Seiffert’s team compared 360 of them.

B.recipe: right case, misread finding (SWAP)
B.why_wrong: Darwinius was reclassified, but the text says that it, not monkeys and apes, belongs with relatives of lemurs, and that the traits it shares with monkeys came from convergent evolution.

C.recipe: right case, lesson overgeneralized (BROAD)
C.why_wrong: The text does say the traits Darwinius shares with monkeys came from “convergent evolution,” but it draws no rule about how often shared traits arise that way. The lesson it states concerns completeness: a nearly intact skeleton “does not by itself settle where a species belongs in evolutionary history.”

sources.what: Seiffert, Perry, Simons, Boyer 2009, Nature: Darwinius “widely publicised as an important link in the early evolution of Anthropoidea”; analysis of 360 features across 117 primates places adapiforms as sister taxa of crown Strepsirrhini, with Darwinius in an extinct caenopithecine clade, and its anthropoid-like features as convergences

items.notes: Area: natural science (paleontology). Key D. Key parts: 2 (the reclassification; to illustrate that completeness does not settle relationships). Section 6 checks: key 22 words; options 22 to 25 words; distractors with a true first clause and a false later clause: A, B and C (3 of 3). The passage’s evaluative close is the author’s lesson drawn from the case; the source states the reclassification and the convergence reading. Age (47 million years) and find place (Messel, Germany) are background.
band7_moves: dual, hedged purpose (“discusses ... to illustrate why”) in the manner of c61a7c4a, with the evaluative point placed last instead of first
the distractors keep the case and change its purpose: a critique of publicity, a misread finding about monkeys and lemurs, a dating goal for a true method
key abstracts the lesson (“completeness is not enough to establish its evolutionary relationships”) away from the passage’s wording

fixes: key paraphrased away from the closing sentence
C (wholly invented goal) replaced by an overgeneralized convergent-evolution lesson
A lengthened slightly

band7.why: P_view on c61a7c4a: hedged dual purpose (reclassification, to illustrate a caution) paraphrased away from the closing sentence; all three distractors keep the case and fail on the purpose (publicity, lemurs, overgeneralized convergence).

items.passage: In 2015, composer Max Richter released Sleep, a composition exceeding eight hours that he conceived with his partner, the visual artist Yulia Mahr, to accompany an entire night’s rest. While composing it, Richter consulted neuroscientist David Eagleman about how the brain functions during sleep, and he structured the piece as 31 unhurried sections for piano, strings, organ, soprano voice, and electronics; the work was performed overnight in London that year for an audience reclining in beds rather than seated in rows. One reviewer, however, objected that the title was excessively prescriptive, instructing listeners how to experience music that plainly had other uses.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It introduces a lengthy musical work meant for an unusual listening situation, details how the work was created and presented, and then relays one critic’s objection to its title.

It presents a composer’s project designed for an unusual listening situation, describes the scientific advice that shaped it, and then reports a scientist’s doubts about whether the work helps people sleep.
It describes an overnight performance of a lengthy musical work, explains how listeners reacted to hearing it from beds, and then argues that the work deserves a wider audience.
It introduces a collaboration between a composer and an artist, compares their contributions to a lengthy work, and then summarizes critics’ praise for its structure.
items.explanation: The first sentence introduces Sleep, “a composition exceeding eight hours” meant “to accompany an entire night’s rest.” The next sentence details how it was made (Richter “consulted neuroscientist David Eagleman” and “structured the piece as 31 unhurried sections”) and how it was presented (“for an audience reclining in beds”). The last sentence relays a reviewer’s objection that “the title was excessively prescriptive.” Choice A follows these three moves.

B.recipe: first two moves right, third move invented (INV)
B.why_wrong: The text does describe Eagleman’s advice, but the closing objection comes from “one reviewer” and concerns the title; no scientist doubts whether the work helps people sleep.

C.recipe: first move partial, later moves invented (PART)
C.why_wrong: The overnight performance is only one detail; the text does not describe listeners’ reactions and never argues that the work deserves a wider audience.

D.recipe: first move partly right, later moves invented (INV)
D.why_wrong: Mahr is mentioned as Richter’s collaborator, but the text never compares their contributions, and the critic it cites objects to the title rather than praising the structure.

sources.what: Sleep (Max Richter album): conceived with Yulia Mahr to fit a full night’s sleep, Richter consulted neuroscientist David Eagleman; about 8 h 24 min in 31 slow-tempo sections for piano, strings, organ, soprano, synthesizers and electronics; 2015 Wellcome Collection performance from midnight to 8 AM with the audience in beds; Pitchfork’s reviewer found the title “simply too didactic as a name”, telling “us how to enjoy something that clearly has other uses”

items.notes: Area: humanities (music). Key A. Planned band_target 7, written as band 6: S14 has no band-7 official item (3.9 is band 5), per WAVE.md. Band-6 moves: three-move structure; B keeps moves 1 and 2 and breaks move 3 (the critic made a scientist); C and D break later moves. Reviewer left unnamed; his point paraphrased from the quotation in the source.

band7.why: S14 has no band-7 official item (3.9 is band 5), so it cannot be band 7; a three-move structure where B breaks only move 3 makes it a strong band 6.

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Sarah Pratt McLean’s 1881 novel Cape Cod Folks. The narrator, who has just come to a Cape Cod village as its schoolteacher, is at an evening meeting where a speaker has been delivering a fiery warning.

Among the usually restless audience, there was a moment of almost breathless suspense. Not half a mile away, behind a strip of cedar woods, we could plainly hear the surf rolling in from the bay, breaking hard against the shore with its awful, monotonous moan, moan, moan.

My heart was already faint with home-sickness. The effect of that waiting moment was as sombre as anything I had ever experienced. Much to my distaste, I found myself sympathizing with the vague terror and unrest around me.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To show that the narrator fears that the sea will soon flood the village while the meeting is under way
To portray the narrator being drawn, against her wishes, into the anxious mood of a gathering
To describe the speaker’s skill at holding the attention of a usually restless audience
To explain why the narrator has become homesick since arriving in the village
items.explanation: The text describes “a moment of almost breathless suspense” at the meeting and the “awful, monotonous moan” of the surf. The narrator then says that “much to my distaste, I found myself sympathizing with the vague terror and unrest around me.” The main purpose is therefore to portray the narrator being drawn, against her wishes, into the gathering’s anxious mood, as choice B says.

A.recipe: word hook, literalized image (LIT)
A.why_wrong: The narrator hears the surf, but she never says she fears a flood; the “terror” she shares is a “vague” unease in the room, and she sympathizes with it only “much to my distaste.”

C.recipe: partial, shifted focus (PART)
C.why_wrong: The text mentions the audience’s “breathless suspense,” but its focus is the narrator’s response, not the speaker’s skill, which the excerpt never describes.

D.recipe: detail made into the purpose, invented cause (INV)
D.why_wrong: The narrator says her heart “was already faint with home-sickness,” but the text never explains why, and the homesickness is one detail in a description of the moment at the meeting.

sources.what: McLean (later Greene), Cape Cod Folks (1881), chapter 1, checked against Gutenberg 19708; the narrator is “the Wallencamp school-teacher”; excerpt begins after “But Aunt Sibylla paused.”

items.notes: Literature (novel, 1881; published under the name Sarah Pratt McLean). Key B. Excerpt copied exactly from two consecutive paragraphs; the first paragraph’s opening sentence (“But Aunt Sibylla paused.”) dropped, hence “adapted”. Context line written from chapter 1 (the speaker’s exhortation and the narrator’s post as teacher).

items.passage: Pad thai, the stir-fried rice noodle dish sold by street vendors throughout Thailand, is often assumed to have been part of the country’s cuisine for centuries. <u>Historian Mark Padoongpatt, however, traces the dish to the late 1930s and early 1940s, when the government of Prime Minister Plaek Phibunsongkhram promoted rice noodles as part of a campaign to build a modern national identity</u>. The dish’s history therefore illustrates how a national cuisine can be shaped by deliberate political decisions as well as by long-standing custom.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It identifies the long-standing custom that the following sentence contrasts with deliberate political decisions.
It explains why the assumption described in the previous sentence first became widespread.
It provides historical details that support the generalization presented in the following sentence.
It describes a disagreement among historians that the following sentence resolves.
items.explanation: The underlined sentence reports that Padoongpatt “traces the dish to the late 1930s and early 1940s,” when the government “promoted rice noodles as part of a campaign to build a modern national identity.” The following sentence generalizes from that history: a national cuisine “can be shaped by deliberate political decisions as well as by long-standing custom.” The underlined sentence therefore supplies the historical details that support that generalization.

A.recipe: wrong relation, reversed content (REV)
A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence describes a government campaign, which is an example of “deliberate political decisions,” not of “long-standing custom.”

B.recipe: invented cause (INV)
B.why_wrong: The text never explains why people came to assume that pad thai is centuries old; the underlined sentence challenges that assumption instead.

D.recipe: invented relation (REL)
D.why_wrong: Only one historian is mentioned, and the text describes no disagreement for the following sentence to resolve.

sources.what: Pad thai: Thailand’s rice shortage during the war led Plaek Phibunsongkhram’s government to promote rice noodles, helping establish the modern identity of Thailand; historian Mark Padoongpatt: the dish “was called pad thai as a way to galvanize nationalism”

items.notes: Area: history (food history, Thailand). Key C. Attributed to Padoongpatt because the source gives the Phibun-era origin as his account and the commonly held explanation; dates rounded to Phibun’s first premiership (1938 to 1944). Review: CB puts the period inside the underline in all 22 tagged “underlined sentence” items; moved inside, check_rw’s sentence splitter merged sentences (medium 37.7 words per sentence against CB 30.0, gate 34.5), so it stays outside until the splitter strips <u> tags.

items.passage: Manta rays feed by swimming with their mouths open, straining plankton from the water as it flows across filtering structures at the back of the mouth. Although the pores in these structures are larger than many of the particles the rays consume, the filters capture those particles efficiently and seldom become clogged. Using physical models and computer simulations of water flow, Misty Paig-Tran and her colleagues found that <u>particles strike the filters’ wing-like lobes and ricochet away from the pores</u>, so that the rays retain small prey while water passes through quickly.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the mechanism that allows manta rays to filter small prey efficiently.
It describes the method the researchers used to model the rays’ feeding structures.
It identifies the reason that manta rays feed on plankton rather than on larger prey.
It explains why the pores in manta rays’ filters are larger than the particles the rays eat.
items.explanation: The second sentence sets up a puzzle: the pores are “larger than many of the particles the rays consume,” yet the filters “capture those particles efficiently and seldom become clogged.” The underlined portion explains how: “particles strike the filters’ wing-like lobes and ricochet away from the pores.” It therefore describes the mechanism that lets the rays filter small prey efficiently.

B.recipe: neighbor’s content (PART)
B.why_wrong: The researchers’ method (“physical models and computer simulations of water flow”) appears just before the underlined portion; the portion itself states what they found.

C.recipe: invented cause (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text never compares plankton with larger prey or explains the rays’ choice of food.

D.recipe: word hook, invented explanation (LIT)
D.why_wrong: The text states that the pores are larger than many particles but never explains why; the underlined portion explains how the filters work despite the pore size.

sources.what: Divi, Strother, Paig-Tran 2018, Science Advances: physical modeling and computational fluid dynamics show manta rays use ricochet separation, in which particles intercepted by wing-like structures ricochet away from the filter pores, separating particles smaller than the pore size, allowing high flow and resisting clogging

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine biology, biomechanics). Key A. Paig-Tran is the senior author of the 2018 paper.

Hocket is hardly confined to that tradition, however: ethnomusicologists have documented it in the music of several African peoples, including the Ba-Benzélé of Central Africa and the Gogo of Tanzania, whose performers weave short vocal or instrumental figures into a single line.

items.passage: Utopian fiction, such as Thomas More’s Utopia (1516) and Tommaso Campanella’s The City of the Sun (1602), typically presents an ideal society through the report of a traveler who has visited it. Critics have observed that this device allows such works to describe a society’s laws and customs at length while saying little about how readers’ own societies might come to resemble it. Some utopian works, however, also narrate the transition: in a chapter of William Morris’s News from Nowhere (1890) titled “How the Change Came,” an elderly man explains to a visitor from the nineteenth century how his society arose.

items.explanation: The text first characterizes utopian fiction, naming Utopia and The City of the Sun and noting that such works present an ideal society “through the report of a traveler.” It adds that such works say “little about how readers’ own societies might come to resemble it,” and then notes that “some utopian works, however, also narrate the transition,” as in News from Nowhere. A.why_wrong: The text names two works but never compares them or calls either more realistic.

C.recipe: invented history and ranking (INV)

items.passage: Why do some fragments of ancient Roman glass shimmer with brilliant, shifting colors? Such iridescence is common on excavated glass and is a familiar sign of aging. Examining one fragment that reflects light almost like a gold mirror, Giulia Guidetti, Fiorenzo Omenetto, and their colleagues found that its surface had slowly weathered over the centuries and that silica had then settled back onto it in extremely thin, highly ordered layers. Those layers, the researchers concluded, reflect only certain colors of light, so the fragment’s color comes from the structure of its surface rather than from any pigment.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: The text asks why some ancient objects have a certain appearance and then describes research that suggests an explanation for it.
The text asks why some ancient objects have a certain appearance and then explains why researchers have been unable to answer that question.
The text describes how glass was made in ancient Rome and then compares those methods with the ones that glassmakers use today.
The text presents a common belief about ancient glass and then reports a finding that contradicts that belief.
items.explanation: The text opens with a question: “Why do some fragments of ancient Roman glass shimmer with brilliant, shifting colors?” It then describes how Guidetti, Omenetto, and their colleagues examined one fragment and ends with their conclusion that the thin layers on its surface “reflect only certain colors of light,” so the color “comes from the structure of its surface rather than from any pigment.” The text therefore asks why some ancient objects look a certain way and then presents research that suggests an explanation.

B.recipe: first move right, second move reversed (REV)
B.why_wrong: The text does ask why the glass shimmers, but the researchers did reach an answer: the layers on the fragment’s surface “reflect only certain colors of light.”

C.recipe: wholly wrong template (INV)
C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how Roman glass was made or about modern glassmaking; it explains how one fragment’s surface changed long after it was made.

D.recipe: wholly wrong template (INV)
D.why_wrong: The text opens with a question, not a common belief, and the finding it reports explains the shimmer rather than contradicting anything; it fits the statement that iridescence is “a familiar sign of aging.”

items.passage: Phoenician ceramic flasks circulated through a regional commercial network in the southern Levant during the early Iron Age, roughly the eleventh to the mid-ninth century BCE. Using gas chromatography to analyze organic residues absorbed into the walls of 27 such flasks from five archaeological sites in Israel, Dvory Namdar and colleagues detected cinnamaldehyde, a principal component of cinnamon, in 10 of them. Because the cinnamon tree grew exclusively in South and Southeast Asia in antiquity, the researchers propose that, provided the compound derived from cinnamon bark, the flasks may indicate long-distance trade with that region.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: It explains how researchers determined that Phoenician flasks recovered at sites in Israel had originally been manufactured in South and Southeast Asia.
It describes an analysis of residues preserved in ancient flasks and explains why the results led researchers to revise the dates previously assigned to the flasks.
It presents a chemical study of ancient containers whose results, if correctly interpreted, suggest a trade connection that spanned a great distance.
It summarizes research on early Iron Age flasks that identified the main routes by which Phoenician goods spread across the southern Levant.
items.explanation: The text describes how Namdar and colleagues analyzed “organic residues absorbed into the walls of 27 such flasks” and detected cinnamaldehyde, “a principal component of cinnamon,” in 10 of them. It then notes that “the cinnamon tree grew exclusively in South and Southeast Asia in antiquity,” so the researchers propose that, “provided the compound derived from cinnamon bark, the flasks may indicate long-distance trade with that region.” The text therefore presents a chemical study whose results, if correctly interpreted, suggest a trade connection across a great distance, as choice C says.

A.recipe: SWAP: right study, the far-off origin moved from the cinnamon to the flasks
A.why_wrong: The text says the cinnamon tree grew in South and Southeast Asia; it says nothing about where the flasks themselves were made and calls them “Phoenician ceramic flasks.”

B.recipe: INV: first part true, invented result (redating)
B.why_wrong: The text does describe a residue analysis, but the dates it gives for the flasks are background; nothing suggests the study changed them.

D.recipe: INV: first part true, invented finding built on the word “network”
D.why_wrong: The text mentions that the flasks circulated through “a regional commercial network,” but the study identified a substance inside them, not the routes by which goods moved.

sources.what: Namdar, Gilboa, Neumann, Finkelstein, Weiner 2013, Mediterranean Archaeology and Archaeometry 13(2): lipid residues in 27 early Iron Age (11th to mid-9th c. BCE) Phoenician flasks from five sites in Israel analyzed by GC-MS; 10 contained cinnamaldehyde; the cinnamon tree grew only in South and Southeast Asia in antiquity, so long-distance trade is possible if the compound came from cinnamon bark

items.notes: Area: history and archaeological science. Key C. Band 6 (P_study has a band-7 item, but the plan sets this cell to 6). items.passage:
The following text is adapted from George Crabbe’s 1783 poem “The Village.” Earlier in the poem, the speaker observes that poets have long portrayed the lives of country people as carefree.

I grant indeed that fields and flocks have charms
For him that grazes or for him that farms;
But, when amid such pleasing scenes I trace
The poor laborious natives of the place,
And see the mid-day sun, with fervid ray,
On their bare heads and dewy temples play;
While some, with feebler heads and fainter hearts,
Deplore their fortune, yet sustain their parts:
Then shall I dare these real ills to hide
In tinsel trappings of poetic pride?
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To convey the speaker’s reluctance to conceal the hardships of rural laborers behind ornamental poetic language
To praise rural laborers for enduring their difficult lives without ever expressing discontent about them
To argue that the countryside offers pleasures to visitors that the people who farm the land are unable to appreciate
To express the speaker’s regret that he lacks the skill to describe rural scenes as vividly as other poets have done
items.explanation: The speaker grants that “fields and flocks have charms,” but when he sees “the poor laborious natives of the place” working under “the mid-day sun,” some of whom “deplore their fortune,” he asks, “Then shall I dare these real ills to hide / In tinsel trappings of poetic pride?” The question implies that he will not hide these “real ills” behind showy, flattering verse. The text therefore conveys the speaker’s reluctance to conceal rural laborers’ hardships behind ornamental poetic language.

B.recipe: PART plus REV: true that some laborers endure, false that none complain
B.why_wrong: Some laborers “sustain their parts,” but the same line says they “deplore their fortune,” so they do express discontent; and the speaker’s point concerns how poets should portray them, not praise for their silence.

C.recipe: STANCE plus INV: an argument and a visitor-versus-farmer contrast the text never makes
C.why_wrong: The speaker grants that the countryside has charms “for him that grazes or for him that farms,” that is, for the people who work it; he never claims they cannot appreciate those charms.

D.recipe: LIT: “tinsel trappings of poetic pride” literalized into a lack of skill
D.why_wrong: The speaker does not doubt his own skill; he questions whether he should decorate “real ills” with “tinsel trappings,” which other poets use and he rejects.

sources.what: George Crabbe, The Village (1783), Book I, lines 39 to 48, text as printed in George Crabbe: Poems, Volume 1, ed. Adolphus William Ward (Cambridge, 1905); the editor’s variants list gives “gazes” for “grazes” in line 40 of the 1783 first edition, the only change in these lines, hence “adapted”

items.notes: Area: literature (poem, 1783). Key A. Band 6 (hard P_lit band-6 models 3.15 and 3.19 are poems; band-7 model 3.3). Crabbe appears nowhere in the bank or in any official item. Context line is accurate: lines 7 to 38 of Book I criticize pastoral poets who sing “of happy swains, / Because the Muses never knew their pains.” Distractors: B partly right (endurance) and wrong on “never expressing discontent”; C an argument built on the farm line; D literalizes the closing image. Key verb convey; key not the longest option.

band7.why: Pre-1800 verse whose closing rhetorical question must be read as a refusal; B is half right (the laborers endure) and fails on “never expressing discontent”, C misreads the farm line, D literalizes the closing image. Each wrong option falls to one careful reread, as in the band-6 P_lit poems 3.15 and 3.19.

items.passage: Economic historian Jan de Vries has argued that early modern Europe experienced an “industrious revolution”: between about 1600 and 1800, households gave up leisure and redirected their labor toward paid work, spending the proceeds on manufactured goods they had once produced at home. De Vries treats this change and the subsequent Industrial Revolution as parts of a single continuum. Akira Hayami, who coined the term, rejects that interpretation. <u>Hayami had introduced the phrase in 1967 to characterize Tokugawa Japan (1603–1868), where scarce capital produced an economy that absorbed ever more labor, in contrast to Britain’s capital-intensive industrialization.</u>
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It gives an example of the shift from producing goods at home to earning wages that de Vries describes earlier in the text.
It presents a case that de Vries cites in support of his view that industrious and industrial revolutions form a continuum.
It explains why Hayami concluded that Tokugawa Japan never went on to develop an industrial economy.
It clarifies the reasoning behind the objection that the originator of a term raises to another historian’s use of it.
items.explanation: The text says that de Vries treats the industrious revolution and the Industrial Revolution “as parts of a single continuum” and that Hayami, “who coined the term, rejects that interpretation.” The underlined sentence explains why: Hayami used the phrase for a Japanese economy that “absorbed ever more labor, in contrast to Britain’s capital-intensive industrialization,” so for him the two are opposites, not stages of one process. The sentence thus clarifies the reasoning behind Hayami’s objection.

A.recipe: SWAP: a true theme (more labor) assigned to the wrong place and argument
A.why_wrong: The underlined sentence concerns Tokugawa Japan and Hayami’s use of the term, not the European households that de Vries describes, and it offers no example of people giving up home production.

B.recipe: STANCE: right case, wrong holder and reversed role
B.why_wrong: The case of Tokugawa Japan belongs to Hayami, and it is presented as the basis for rejecting the continuum de Vries proposes, not as support for it.

C.recipe: INV: a conclusion about Japan’s later history the text never mentions
C.why_wrong: The text contrasts Japan’s labor-absorbing economy with Britain’s industrialization in the period Hayami studied; it says nothing about whether Japan later industrialized.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Industrious Revolution: term coined by Akira Hayami in a 1967 work to contrast labor-intensive Tokugawa Japan (1603 to 1868), whose path absorbed increasing labor because capital was scarce, with the capital-intensive British Industrial Revolution; Jan de Vries’s version for early modern Europe (about 1600 to 1800): households shift labor to market work, reduce leisure and buy commercially produced goods; Hayami objects that de Vries treats the industrious and industrial revolutions as a continuum, while he sees them as opposing concepts

items.notes: Area: social science (economic history). Key D. Band 6; modelled on 9b01bcf4 (3.10, “helps explain Cruse’s position”) and 2e744883 (3.12). The deciding sentence (“rejects that view”) precedes the span, and the span itself must be read as the reason for it.

Near the section 5 F_example recipe, but each wrong option still falls to one stated fact; plan target 6 met.

items.passage: Hortus Malabaricus, a twelve-volume botanical survey describing more than 700 plants of the Malabar Coast in present-day Kerala, India, began appearing in Amsterdam in 1678. It bears the name of its compiler, Hendrik van Rheede, the Dutch colonial administrator of Malabar, but its contents depend substantially on indigenous expertise: Itty Achudan, a traditional physician from Kerala’s Ezhava community, selected the specimens to be illustrated and dictated their descriptions and medicinal applications in Malayalam, and three Konkani Brahmin physicians subsequently verified the material. The volumes record each plant’s name in Malayalam, Konkani, and Arabic in addition to Latin.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To explain how a colonial governor’s botanical research changed the way plants were named in European scientific works
To describe a seventeenth-century botanical work and show the large part local practitioners played in producing it
To compare the plant knowledge of healers in Kerala with that of the European scholars who later published it
To argue that a celebrated botanical work owes far less to its Dutch compiler than historians have generally recognized
items.explanation: The text first describes Hortus Malabaricus, “a twelve-volume botanical survey describing more than 700 plants of the Malabar Coast.” It then explains that although the work “bears the name of its compiler,” its “contents depend substantially on indigenous expertise”: Itty Achudan selected the specimens and dictated their descriptions, and “three Konkani Brahmin physicians subsequently verified the material.” The text therefore describes a seventeenth-century botanical work and shows the large part local practitioners played in producing it.

A.recipe: INV plus BROAD: an influence on European naming the text never claims
A.why_wrong: The text says the volumes record plant names in several languages, but it never says the work changed how plants were named in European science, and it credits the contents to local experts rather than to van Rheede’s own research.

C.recipe: INV: a comparison of two bodies of knowledge that the text does not make
C.why_wrong: The text says what the local experts contributed; it never describes any separate knowledge held by European scholars, so there is no comparison.

D.recipe: STANCE plus INV: the key’s point recast as an argument against historians
D.why_wrong: The text does say the contents “depend substantially on indigenous expertise,” but it reports this neutrally; it never calls the work celebrated or claims that historians have failed to recognize the experts’ role.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Hortus Malabaricus: 12 volumes compiled by Hendrik van Rheede, governor of Dutch Malabar, published in Amsterdam from 1678; more than 742 plants, 794 copperplate engravings; Itty Achudan, an Ezhava physician, disclosed the knowledge, his team selected the plants to be drawn, and he dictated the material in Malayalam, which was translated into Latin; the material was scrutinized by three Konkani Brahmins (Ranga Bhat, Vinayaka Pandit, Appu Bhat); plant names recorded in Malayalam, Konkani and Arabic besides Latin

items.passage: Little brown bats infected with the fungus responsible for white-nose syndrome die in great numbers during hibernation, and DeeAnn Reeder and colleagues found evidence suggesting why: infected bats arouse from hibernation more frequently than uninfected bats, and each arousal to a warm body temperature depletes fat reserves the animals need to survive the winter. Indiana, northern, and tricolored bats have likewise suffered severe winter mortality from the disease. The big brown bat (Eptesicus fuscus) is an exception: it is highly resistant to infection, which researchers have linked partly to fatty acids in its wing skin that inhibit the fungus’s growth.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It reports and explains a finding about a disease’s effect on one species, notes that other species are similarly affected, and then presents a resistant species and a possible reason for its resistance.

It presents a study showing how and why a disease harms one bat species, indicates that other species have suffered in the same way, and then describes an exception that undermines the study’s explanation.

It describes and accounts for the harm a disease causes one species, extends that observation to several related species, and then predicts that those species will gradually acquire resistance to the disease.
It reports a finding about a disease’s effect on one species, attributes that finding to a flaw in the way the study was designed, and then describes a species that resists the disease.
items.explanation: The text first reports that infected little brown bats “die in great numbers during hibernation” and explains why, citing Reeder and colleagues’ evidence: infected bats “arouse from hibernation more frequently than uninfected bats,” and each arousal “depletes fat reserves the animals need to survive the winter.” It then notes that “Indiana, northern, and tricolored bats have likewise suffered severe winter mortality.” Finally, it presents the big brown bat as “an exception” that “is highly resistant to infection” and gives a possible reason, fatty acids “that inhibit the fungus’s growth.” Choice A describes this structure.

B.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 a stance flip (exception undermines the explanation)
B.why_wrong: The big brown bat’s resistance to infection does not challenge the explanation that frequent arousals deplete infected bats’ fat; the text simply presents the species as an exception and links its resistance to fatty acids in its skin.

C.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 an invented prediction
C.why_wrong: The text never predicts that the affected species will develop resistance; the only resistant species it mentions is the big brown bat, which it presents as an exception.

D.recipe: move 2 invented (methodological flaw)
D.why_wrong: The text presents Reeder and colleagues’ evidence as reliable and uses it to explain the bats’ deaths; it never suggests that the research was flawed.

sources.what: Reeder et al. 2012, PLoS ONE 7(6): e38920: dataloggers on 504 little brown bats; WNS-affected bats aroused to euthermic temperatures more frequently than unaffected bats, likely contributing to mortality; arousals are normal but deplete fat stores

Ingala, Ravenelle, Monro, Frank 2017, PLoS ONE 12(10): e0187195: WNS greatly increases over-winter mortality of little brown, Indiana, northern and tricolored bats; big brown bats (Eptesicus fuscus) are highly resistant to Pd infections; wing-epidermis fatty acids (four of which, and 1-oleoglycerol found in E. fuscus, inhibit Pd growth)

items.passage: From about 1980, tracking data from the Pioneer 10 and 11 spacecraft revealed a puzzling discrepancy: as both probes traveled outward, they were slowing slightly more than predicted, as if subject to a faint, constant sunward acceleration. Drag from interplanetary gas and dust was considered, but the measured density of that material is too low to produce it. An unrecognized gravitational influence fares no better, since the orbits of the outer planets show no corresponding deviation. Slava Turyshev and colleagues’ 2012 reanalysis offers the most compelling account: heat radiated unevenly from the spacecraft generated a recoil force matching the anomaly.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a puzzling measurement, explains why two proposed causes of it are untenable, and then attributes the measurement to errors in the way the spacecraft were tracked.
It describes an unexpected observation, discusses two explanations for it that the author finds unconvincing, and then states that a satisfactory account of it has yet to emerge.
It reports an astronomical finding, presents two competing accounts of it that the author considers equally plausible, and then describes a study that combined those accounts.
It introduces an unexplained effect on the motion of two spacecraft, explains why two candidate causes can be dismissed, and then endorses a later study’s explanation.
items.explanation: The text opens with an anomaly: the Pioneer probes “were slowing slightly more than predicted.” It then dismisses two candidate causes, drag, because “the measured density of that material is too low to produce it,” and an unrecognized gravitational influence, because “the orbits of the outer planets show no corresponding deviation.” Finally, it calls Turyshev and colleagues’ 2012 reanalysis “the most compelling account,” endorsing their explanation that unevenly radiated heat “generated a recoil force matching the anomaly.” Choice D describes this structure.

A.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 invented (tracking errors)
A.why_wrong: The text never says the anomaly came from tracking errors; the account it favors is a real physical force, “a recoil force” produced by unevenly radiated heat.

B.recipe: moves 1 and 2 right, move 3 reversed (no account yet)
B.why_wrong: The author does not say that a convincing account is still missing; the text calls Turyshev and colleagues’ 2012 reanalysis “the most compelling account.”

C.recipe: move 2 stance flip (equally plausible) and move 3 invented
C.why_wrong: The author rejects both drag and an unrecognized gravitational influence rather than considering them plausible, and the favored study does not combine them; it attributes the anomaly to heat.

Turyshev, Toth, Kinsella, Lee, Lok, Ellis 2012, Physical Review Letters 108, 241101 (arXiv 1204.2507), Support for the thermal origin of the Pioneer anomaly: thermal recoil force from anisotropic emission of heat; once accounted for, no anomalous acceleration remains

items.passage:
The following text is adapted from Edmund Gosse’s 1907 memoir Father and Son, in which Gosse recalls an incident from his early childhood.

I confused [my father] in some sense with God; at all events I believed that my Father knew everything and saw everything. One morning in my sixth year, my Mother and I were alone in the morning-room, when my Father came in and announced some fact to us. The shock to me was as that of a thunderbolt, for what my Father had said “was not true.” My Mother gently told him so, and he accepted the correction. Nothing could possibly have been more trifling to my parents, but to me it meant an epoch.
items.stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
options: To describe how the narrator’s mother taught him to question the things his father told him
To recount how a seemingly trivial event overturned a young child’s belief that his father knew everything
To show that the narrator’s parents frequently disagreed about what had actually happened
To convey the narrator’s fear that he would be punished for pointing out his father’s error
items.explanation: The narrator says that as a child he “believed that my Father knew everything and saw everything.” He then describes a morning when his father announced something that “was not true,” and his mother corrected him. Although “nothing could possibly have been more trifling to my parents,” for the narrator “it meant an epoch.” The text therefore recounts how a seemingly trivial event overturned the child’s belief that his father knew everything.

A.recipe: SWAP plus INV: the mother’s one correction turned into a lesson for the child
A.why_wrong: The mother corrects the father, not the child, and she does so “gently” on one occasion; the text never says she taught the narrator to question his father.

C.recipe: BROAD: one mild correction stretched into frequent disagreement
C.why_wrong: The text describes a single “trifling” correction that the father “accepted”; it never says the parents often disagreed.

D.recipe: INV: a fear of punishment the text never mentions
D.why_wrong: The narrator does not point out the error; his mother does. His shock comes from discovering that his father could be wrong, not from fear of being punished.

sources.what: Edmund Gosse, Father and Son (1907), chapter II, the incident in his sixth year; text copied from Project Gutenberg #2540, trimmed at sentence boundaries (the sentence about the narrator standing on the rug and looking into the fire, and the one about mother and son knowing the facts, left out), “[my father]” replaces “him”, single quotes made double with the period moved inside

Gosse appears nowhere in the bank or the official items. Distractors: A SWAP (who corrects whom), C BROAD, D INV. Key paraphrases “trifling” and “epoch” (seemingly trivial event; overturned a belief).

items.passage: In his 1935 book Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact, Polish microbiologist Ludwik Fleck argued that scientific knowledge is produced collectively, within communities of researchers whose shared assumptions shape what they observe; he called such communities “thought collectives.” <u>Fleck’s central case was the history of the Wassermann reaction, a diagnostic blood test for syphilis.</u> Although August von Wassermann later remembered the test’s development as a direct path toward a goal he had planned from the start, Fleck maintained that it had actually emerged through a meandering, collective process marked by exchanges and misunderstandings.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces a medical test that, according to Fleck, Wassermann developed without help from other researchers.
It explains why the communities of researchers described in the previous sentence seldom agreed about the value of the test.
It identifies the main example that Fleck used to illustrate the view described in the previous sentence.
It describes a discovery that Fleck credited with first leading him to study how scientific knowledge is produced.
items.explanation: The first sentence presents Fleck’s argument that “scientific knowledge is produced collectively, within communities of researchers,” which he called “thought collectives.” The underlined sentence names “Fleck’s central case,” the history of the Wassermann reaction, and the last sentence shows how that history fits his argument: Wassermann “later remembered the test’s development as a direct path,” but Fleck maintained that it “had actually emerged through a meandering, collective process.” The underlined sentence therefore identifies the main example that Fleck used to illustrate the view described in the previous sentence.

A.recipe: REV: the collective process Fleck describes turned into a lone achievement
A.why_wrong: Fleck maintained that the test “had actually emerged through a meandering, collective process”; it was Wassermann’s later memory, not Fleck, that presented the work as “a direct path toward a goal he had planned from the start.”

B.recipe: INV: a disagreement about the test’s value the text never mentions
B.why_wrong: The text mentions “exchanges and misunderstandings” during the test’s development, but it never says researchers disagreed about the test’s value, and the underlined sentence explains nothing about the communities in the previous sentence.

D.recipe: INV: a causal origin the text never claims
D.why_wrong: The text calls the Wassermann reaction “Fleck’s central case,” the example he used to support his argument; it never says the test first led him to study how scientific knowledge is produced.

sources.what: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Ludwik Fleck: Genesis and Development of a Scientific Fact (1935); cognition is a collective activity and facts emerge within thought collectives shaped by thought styles; syphilis research and the Wassermann reaction are his central case; success is achievable only if the whole group of scholars is engaged; after fifteen years an identification between results and intentions had taken place in Wassermann’s thinking, so the meandering process of development came to look a straight, goal-directed path

items.passage: Vincent van Gogh frequently painted over his earlier work, and roughly 30 percent of his paintings are thought to conceal other compositions. Conventional imaging methods had detected only the vague outline of a head beneath his Patch of Grass (1887), too indistinct to reveal any facial features. <u>To obtain a clearer view, Joris Dik and colleagues scanned a section of the canvas with an intense synchrotron X-ray beam, which caused the chemical elements in the concealed paint layer to emit characteristic radiation.</u> Maps of mercury, from the red pigment vermilion, and of antimony were then combined into a color image of a woman’s face.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It describes the technique researchers used to reveal an image hidden beneath a painting’s surface.
It explains why van Gogh frequently painted over his earlier work rather than starting each new painting on a fresh canvas.
It identifies the pigments van Gogh used when he painted the landscape visible in Patch of Grass.
It presents evidence that challenges an earlier claim about who painted the concealed portrait.
items.explanation: The text explains that conventional imaging methods detected only “the vague outline of a head” beneath Patch of Grass. The underlined sentence then tells how Dik and colleagues “scanned a section of the canvas with an intense synchrotron X-ray beam,” which made the elements in “the concealed paint layer” emit radiation, and the last sentence reports the result, “a color image of a woman’s face.” The underlined sentence thus describes the technique researchers used to reveal an image hidden beneath a painting’s surface.

B.recipe: PART: restates the first sentence’s topic and adds an invented reason
B.why_wrong: The first sentence says van Gogh often painted over earlier work, but no sentence explains why, and the underlined sentence concerns the researchers’ scan.

C.recipe: SWAP: the hidden layer’s elements given to the visible landscape
C.why_wrong: The scan detected elements in “the concealed paint layer,” the portrait beneath the landscape; the text says nothing about the pigments in the visible grass painting.

D.recipe: STANCE plus INV: a dispute about authorship the text never mentions
D.why_wrong: The text raises no question about who painted the hidden portrait; it is presented as van Gogh’s own earlier work beneath the landscape.

items.passage: In 1903, ceramic artist Mary Chase Perry Stratton and her business partner, Horace Caulkins, founded Pewabic Pottery in Detroit, Michigan. Caulkins, a specialist in high-temperature kilns, designed the Revelation kiln, and the studio soon became known for its shimmering, iridescent glazes. Those glazes can still be seen on tiles in buildings such as the Detroit Public Library and the Basilica of the National Shrine of the Immaculate Conception in Washington, DC. Designated a National Historic Landmark in 1991, Pewabic continues to operate today as a nonprofit educational institution that offers ceramics classes, holds exhibitions, and sells pottery made on site.
items.stem: Which choice best describes the overall purpose of the text?
options: To explain how Pewabic Pottery’s glazes changed the design of public buildings across the United States
To compare the contributions that Pewabic Pottery’s two founders made to the studio’s early success
To describe the methods Pewabic Pottery uses today to teach ceramics to students
To trace the history of a ceramics studio from its founding to the present day
items.explanation: The text begins with Pewabic Pottery’s founding “in 1903,” describes the studio’s kiln and “iridescent glazes,” names buildings where its tiles “can still be seen,” and ends by noting that Pewabic “continues to operate today as a nonprofit educational institution.” The text therefore traces the history of the studio from its founding to the present day.

A.recipe: BROAD: two buildings stretched to public architecture across the country
A.why_wrong: The text names two buildings with Pewabic tiles; it never says the glazes changed the design of public buildings nationwide.

B.recipe: INV: a comparison the text does not make
B.why_wrong: The text mentions what each founder did, but only in passing, and it never weighs their contributions against each other.

C.recipe: PART: the last sentence only
C.why_wrong: The text says only that Pewabic offers ceramics classes; it never describes how they are taught, and the classes are just one part of the studio’s history.

items.notes: Area: humanities (ceramics, decorative arts). Key D. Medium P_profile modelled on 2.5 (overview of an institution’s founding and later life). Stem is 2.5’s “overall purpose” variant.
